references.text: God uses the plural form 'Let us make man,' which corresponds to 'like one of us' in 3:22.
The introduction of the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil in Eden's garden, both central in 3:22.
The prohibition against eating from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, which sets the stage for human disobedience and God's response in 3:22.
The serpent's promise that humans will become 'like God, knowing good and evil' - direct background to God's statement in 3:22.
Expulsion from the garden and the cherubim guarding the way to the tree of life - the direct follow-up to God's decision in 3:22.
God uses the plural form 'Who will go for us?', parallel to 'like one of us' in Gen 3:22.
The promise to eat from the tree of life in God's paradise, pointing back to the tree of life in Gen 3:22.
The tree of life in the new Jerusalem, showing God's final restoration of access to eternal life.
Those who wash their robes have the right to the tree of life - restoration of what was closed off in Gen 3:22-24.
Both verses illustrate God's limitation of human lifespan as a consequence of sin.
Theological contrast: God's desire for repentance and life (Ezekiel) versus preventing eternal life in sin (Genesis).
Theological contrast: Humanity's fallen knowledge of good and evil (Genesis) versus true wisdom, which is turning away from evil (Job).
Direct narrative connection: 3:22 is the consequence of breaking the command in 3:3.
Theological contrast and fulfillment: Jesus as the new tree of life who gives eternal life, in contrast to being excluded from the tree of life in Eden.
